title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling with Imperfect Judges
claim: Whether best-of-N picks a correct answer depends on the competition between the maxima in the upper tails of two reward distributions.
layout: 1 panel, density curves with sample dots on axis, boxed formula bottom-right
description: A single density plot with reward value on the x-axis and probability density on the y-axis. Two overlapping Gaussian curves are shown. The orange curve is the incorrect-response reward, centered near -1. The blue curve is the correct-response reward, centered near +1. Both are shaded lightly and have dashed vertical lines at their means. Colored dots along the x-axis mark sampled rewards: orange dots for about n(1-p) incorrect samples and blue dots for about np correct samples. The legend at the top and the key at the upper right give the dot counts. Dashed black lines link the largest orange dot and the largest blue dot to the labels M_w and M_c. A red-bordered box at the bottom right holds the formula Pr(ŷ_bon = y*) = Pr(M_c > M_w). The eye goes first to the two overlapping bell curves, then to the maxima labels and the boxed formula.
caption: An illustrative overview of our explanation of BoN for verifiable problems. When n responses are sampled, assuming pass@1 = p, we obtain approximately np correct responses and n(1 −p) incorrect responses, each assigned a reward according to the corresponding reward distribution. Whether BoN selects a correct response is determined by the competition between the maximum reward Mc among the np correct responses and the maximum reward Mw among the n(1 −p) incorrect responses. When n is sufficiently large, these maxima are governed by the tails of the respective distributions. Thus, the performance of BoN depends on the competition between the tails of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect responses.
abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under imperfect reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N for verifiable problems, which have binary correctness criteria, as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an imperfect selector can be almost polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling.
